Is it safe to swim at Chaweng Beach? | Usually yes from January to September, when the sea is calm and the north end is shallow. From October to December, the north-east monsoon brings big waves and rip currents, and red flags often fly. Never swim when the red flag is up, and keep clear of jet skis.
When do red flags fly on Koh Samui? | Mostly on the east coast (Chaweng and Lamai) from October to December during the north-east monsoon, and during winter cold surges, such as 19 February 2026, when 1–2 m waves closed both beaches. Check the flag every time you swim.
Are there box jellyfish on Koh Samui? | Yes. Nine of the 10 box jellyfish deaths recorded in Thailand since 2002 were in waters off Samui and Koh Phangan. Risk is higher in the rainy months, after heavy rain, in calm water and at night. Many hotels have vinegar stations and warning signs.
What should I do if I'm stung by a jellyfish? | Leave the water and keep still, pour vinegar over the sting for at least 30 seconds, don't rub it or rinse with fresh water, and call 1669. Go to hospital immediately for severe pain, breathing problems or confusion; start CPR if breathing stops.
Which Koh Samui beaches are safest for swimming? | Choeng Mon is one of the calmest all year. Lipa Noi is shallow and gentle at high tide, good for toddlers. Chaweng's north end and Lamai's centre are good from January to September. Avoid Bophut and Big Buddha beaches for swimming.
Are there lifeguards on Koh Samui beaches? | Only on parts of the busiest beaches, mainly Chaweng and Lamai, and not all year. Most Samui beaches, including the coves and the west coast, have no lifeguard, so swim with a friend and stay within your depth.
Why is the water so shallow at some beaches? | The north and west coasts face sheltered, shallow water with a large tidal range. At low tide, beaches such as Bang Por, Lipa Noi and Bang Kao become flats of sand, rock and coral rubble. Swim around high tide and wear water shoes.
~Is it safe to climb on the rocks at Lad Koh? | Not when the sea is rough. Monsoon waves break over the rocks below Lad Koh viewpoint, and a tourist was swept away there in November 2024. Stay on the viewing platform from October to December and whenever waves are big.
